passage:
"Look at this," Tanuja said, waving her phone. "All the money I earned at the design studio, and so much of it goes to tax. The forms make no sense either."

Zeenat looked up from the sofa. "You've been muttering since morning."

"Because it's unfair! The roads are broken and I still pay."

"It is annoying," Zeenat said. "But the due date is Thursday."

"I know. I hate that I know." Tanuja sighed. "Part of me wants to skip it out of spite."

"And then you get a penalty letter and you're angry about that too."

Tanuja laughed a little. "Fine. I'll file, and then I'll go to that ward meeting about local budgets."

"Now that's a plan. Chai while you do the forms?"

"Yes, please. Extra ginger. 🙂"

qa.q: When is the due date, according to Zeenat?
qa.a: Zeenat says the due date is Thursday.

qa.q: What does Tanuja feel about paying tax, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Tanuja feels resentful and thinks it is unfair, shown by the muttering since morning and the line "The roads are broken and I still pay."

qa.q: What could Tanuja do with the resentment besides skipping the filing?
qa.a: File on time and take the grievance to the ward meeting about local budgets, so the anger goes toward change instead of a penalty.

qa.q: Why might Zeenat stay calmer about the forms than Tanuja?
qa.a: Zeenat agrees it is annoying but is looking at the practical side: missing the date brings a penalty letter, which would give Tanuja one more thing to be angry about.

grounding: Tanuja resents the tax system but chooses to comply and to advocate through the ward meeting instead of evading.

passage: Francis, you're grumbling about your first tax return. I know. When I was twenty-five, a young woman running a small tuition centre in Hyderabad, I hated paying. The forms were confusing, and the money went, I thought, into potholes that never got fixed. A friend told me, "Just don't declare the cash students. Nobody will know." I was tempted. My chest was tight with anger every March. But my father had once hidden income from his tea shop, and I'd seen him sick with worry when the notice came. So I paid. And every year I wrote a letter to our ward councillor about the potholes, and later I joined the traders' association that asked for simpler forms. The forms did get a little simpler. The potholes, not so much. You can dislike a system, Francis, and still keep your name clean. That's what your Noor-aunty has learned.

qa.q: What did Noor's friend suggest she not declare?
What was Noor feeling each March?
qa.a: She felt resentful and angry, her chest tight, about paying tax into a system she thought wasted money.

qa.q: What turning point in Noor's story shaped her choice?
qa.a: Remembering her father sick with worry after hiding income led her to pay, while writing to the councillor and joining the traders' association to push for change.

qa.q: How might Noor's father have felt when the notice came?
qa.a: He was probably frightened and ashamed, worried about what the hidden income would cost him.

grounding: An elder recalls resenting taxes, choosing to comply while advocating for change, because evasion turns a grievance into a legal risk.

passage:
It was 11 p.m. on the last day to file the quarterly tax return, and the government portal had crashed for the third time. Mehak sat in her boutique in Amritsar, surrounded by invoices, furious. "They make the rules impossible and then their own website doesn't work!"
Her friend Gurpreet, who ran the shop next door, leaned in the doorway. "Why bother? Half the market doesn't file on time. Just skip this quarter."
Mehak was tempted. She was exhausted and angry. But she remembered the penalty notice her uncle got last year, and how long it took him to sort it out.
"No. I hate it, but I'm filing."
She took a screenshot of the error page with the time showing, then tried again at 11:40. It went through at 11:52. She saved the acknowledgement twice.
The next morning, still irritated, she wrote to the traders' association asking them to raise the portal crashes with the department.

qa.q: What time did Mehak's return finally go through?
What was Mehak feeling as the portal kept crashing?
qa.a: She felt furious and exhausted, resenting rules she saw as impossible when the government's own website failed.

qa.q: How did Mehak handle her resentment wisely?
qa.a: She filed anyway, screenshotted the error as a record, saved the acknowledgement, and asked the traders' association to raise the problem officially.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet see Mehak's choice to file?
qa.a: Gurpreet may think she is being overly careful, but might also notice that she avoided a risk that skipping would bring.

grounding: The protagonist resents complex tax rules and a failing system, but complies and advocates for change instead of evading.
